processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Ingots (each steel melted in a 50 kg high-frequency vacuum induction furnace and cast into a 150 mm diameter ingot) were homogenized at 1200 °C for 5 h before hot rolling; shared fabrication route for the Fe30Mn8Al1C steel.
Hot rolled into rods with a diameter of 16 mm, then air-cooled to room temperature (parent process proc_hot-rolled).

Solution treated at 1100 °C for 2 h followed by water quenching; used to reveal the influence of solution temperature on the Al-series compositions (Fig. 2d, Fig. 8d). Distinctive step of this sample (state 1100 °C–2 h–WQ).

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Mass density measured by the Archimedes drainage method (room temperature)

measurement_conditions.specimen_geometry: standard tensile specimen, gauge length 25 mm and diameter 5 mm, tensile axis parallel to the rod axis
measurement_conditions.other_conditions: This sample: Fe30Mn8Al1C (Al-8) solution treated at 1100 °C for 2 h followed by water quenching; data presented in Fig. 2(d) and Fig. 8(d) for the Al series, no tabulated numerical values for the 1100 °C condition

tensile_properties.stress_strain_curves: Engineering stress-strain curves of the Al-series (6–12% Al) solution treated at 1100 °C for 2 h (Fig. 2d); no numerical values are tabulated for this condition.

strain_hardening_rate.description: Work-hardening-rate curves of the Al-series after 1100 °C/2 h solution treatment (Fig. 8d) retain the ordering seen at 1050 °C (highest rate for 6% Al, lowest for 12% Al), and the true stress-strain curves extend to noticeably larger true strain than after the 1050 °C treatment; no numerical WH-rate values are given for Al-8 at 1100 °C.

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: ambient temperature; initial strain rate 1.1 × 10^-3 s^-1; round specimen gauge length 25 mm, diameter 5 mm, tensile axis parallel to rod axis; two specimens tested and values averaged
characterization_methods.purpose: Measure stress-strain response and strain-hardening rate of the solution-treated low-density steels, including the Al-series after 1100 °C treatment (Fig. 2d, Fig. 8d)
characterization_methods.key_findings: Alloying content mainly changes work-hardening capacity rather than the peak true stress; after 1100 °C solution treatment the Al-series stress-strain curves reach larger true strain than after 1050 °C.

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: at -40 °C; V-notch perpendicular to the rod axis; two solution-treated specimens tested, data averaged
characterization_methods.purpose: Measure impact toughness of solution-treated low-density steels
characterization_methods.key_findings: Impact toughness is mainly controlled by the κ-carbide size; high toughness only for low Al/low C/high Mn compositions (quantitative values reported for the 1050 °C series).

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: EBSD system attached to a field emission gun scanning electron microscope (FEI Quanta 650, Thermo Fisher Scientific)
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: operating voltage 20 kV, step size 0.5 μm; specimens electro-polished in 7% Nital at room temperature; grain size by linear intercept with 15° boundary definition using Channel 5 software
characterization_methods.purpose: Determine phase distribution, austenite grain size and twin-boundary fraction of the solution-treated steels
characterization_methods.key_findings: Microstructural parameters (Table 3) are reported for the Al-series after solution treatment (1050 °C condition).

characterization_methods.technique: transmission electron microscopy (TEM) dark-field imaging and selected-area electron diffraction (SAED)
characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: TEM (Tecnai G2 F20 S-TWIN, Thermo Fisher Scientific) operated at 200 kV
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: thin foils twin-jet electro-polished in 10% perchloric acid + 90% ethanol at 20 V and -20 °C
characterization_methods.purpose: Characterize κ-carbide size/distribution and the κ/γ orientation relationship in the solution-treated steels
characterization_methods.key_findings: κ-carbide size increases with C and Al content and decreases with Mn content; orientation relationship (001)κ || (001)γ (data reported for the 1050 °C series).

computational_details.simulation_method: empirical linear least-squares regression of measured density on alloying content
computational_details.validation_against_experiment: Predicted densities match measurements for the series (e.g. Fe30Mn11Al1.0C predicted 6.6 g/cm3 vs measured 6.6 g/cm3; Fe30Mn11Al1.5C predicted 6.55 vs measured 6.56 g/cm3); a comparison with a previously reported relation shows a much smaller C coefficient.

analytical_models.equation_role: Predicts the mass density (g/cm3) of Fe–Mn–Al–C low-density steels from C, Al and Mn content in mass%
analytical_models.model_note: ρ = 8.10 - 0.102C - 0.10Al - 0.01Mn; fitted to the experimental densities of the studied alloy series, which includes Fe30Mn8Al1C (Al-8).

computational_details.simulation_method: linear regression of yield strength against the square root of κ-carbide size (particle-shear strengthening analysis)
computational_details.validation_against_experiment: Linear dependence of yield strength on d_Car^0.5 was obtained for the solution-treated series; fitted slope 97.1 MPa/nm^1/2 and flow stress at zero carbide contribution ~478 MPa.

analytical_models.equation_role: Describes the shear strength contribution from κ-carbides
analytical_models.model_note: σ_shear = α f^(1/2) d_Car^(1/2); the linear fit R_p0.2 = 478 + 97.1 d_Car^0.5 (Fig. 7a) covers the whole series.

unmapped_findings: Measured chemical composition of the alloy used for this sample (Fe30Mn8Al1C, steel designation 'Al-8', Table 1): C 0.98, Mn 30.22, Al 8.08 (mass%), Fe balance; measured density 6.90 g/cm3.

For this sample (Fe30Mn8Al1C solution treated at 1100 °C/2 h + water quenching) the paper reports only a slight decrease of yield strength relative to the 1050 °C condition (Fig. 2d), attributed to an increase of grain size with increasing solution-treatment temperature; no quantitative values are given.

Important caveat on data attribution: the paper's quantitative mechanical properties (Table 2) and microstructural parameters (Table 3) are explicitly for solution treatment at 1050 °C for 2 h, i.e. they belong to the sibling 1050 °C sample, NOT to this 1100 °C sample. Table 3 caption says 'after solution-treatment' but the text (b0042) fixes that condition at 1050 °C; Table 2 caption explicitly states 1050 °C. These values were therefore not entered into this sample's formal fields.

For context only (values belong to the sibling Al-8/1050 °C condition, NOT this sample): UTS 826 ± 2 MPa, YS 548 ± 4 MPa, UE 74 ± 1.1%, A 74.0 ± 1%, Akv-40 294 ± 11 J, σ_TS 1370 MPa, σ_FS 2154 MPa (Table 2); D_FCC-G/T 28.3 ± 12 μm, f_Tw 50.3%, no BCC/ferrite fraction, D_κ-carbides 0 nm (no κ-carbides detected by TEM) (Table 3).

After the 1100 °C solution treatment the true stress-strain curves of the Al series extend to noticeably larger true strain than after 1050 °C, while the work-hardening-rate ordering (highest for lowest Al content) is retained (Fig. 8d).

The paper's design conclusion relevant to the Al-8 composition: only three steels (Fe30Mn6Al1C 354 J, Fe30Mn8Al1C 294 J, Fe30Mn10Al1C 237 J) possessed high impact toughness, linked to the absence or very small size of κ-carbides (these tabulated toughness values correspond to the 1050 °C treatment).
